Darline Graham in South Carolina; Trump’s tariffs added an estimated 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods inflation; companies that Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have invested in have won more than $6 billion in federal contracts; Kimberly Guilfoyle reportedly urged a Trump donor to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; ICE has investigated more than 150 voter-registration groups ahead of the midterm elections; the World Health Organization couldn’t assess the risk of a possible plague outbreak after a Russian anti-plague institute researcher died of pneumonia of unknown origin; and Trump proposed turning his West Palm Beach golf club into a Camp David-type presidential retreat for future presidents and visiting foreign leaders.
1/ Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton privately blamed the Iran war and high fuel prices for his struggling Senate campaign. “It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” he told donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser, calling affordability “by far our biggest problem.” Paxton also complained that Washington was controlling his campaign messaging. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from D.C.,” Paxton said, adding, “I don’t control message or what we’re doing.” While Paxton claimed that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas “dropped our numbers,” Trump nevertheless is making his third trip to Texas in less than a month to campaign for Paxton. Polls show Democrat James Talarico narrowly ahead despite Republicans spending more than $200 million on the race. Trump won the state by more than 13 points in 2024. (Axios / Politico / CNN / The Hill / The Guardian / Politico / New York Times)
2/ Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers called for an end to Trump’s “tariff war” with Canada, saying “here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy.” Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods in August, prompting retaliatory tariffs that threaten Michigan’s auto industry because it depends on cross-border supply chains. Nevertheless, Trump, who endorsed Rogers, said “I viewed [Rogers] as saying that he thinks Canada should make a deal.” The Cook Political Report rates Rogers’ race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed a “toss-up.” (Politico / CNN / Axios / Reuters / The Hill / Wall Street Journal)
- Sen. Susan Collins distanced herself from Trump and defended her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh in her first debate with Democrat Troy Jackson. Asked whether she would appear with Trump if he campaigned in Maine, Collins said she doubted he would come: “I’m not exactly his favorite senator.” (Bloomberg / Washington Post)
3/ The primary Senate Republican super PAC plans to spend $5 million to defend Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. Trump won the state by about 18 points in 2024. Graham, appointed after her brother Lindsey Graham died in July, faces Democrat Annie Andrews in a race recent polls show is close. Trump, meanwhile, used an anti-trans slur three times to attack Andrews, who is not transgender, while urging South Carolina voters to elect Graham. Democrats need to flip four seats to take control of the Senate. (Axios / Associated Press / Bloomberg / Washington Post / CBS News / NBC News / MS Now / Mediaite)
- The FCC is considering a request by a conservative group to allow political groups to allow unsolicited political robocalls to cellphones, including AI-generated voices. Federal law currently bans most robocalls to cellphones without prior consent. (Associated Press)
4/ Trump’s tariffs added an estimated 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods inflation. Without the tariffs, goods prices would have fallen slightly The estimate reflects the 12 months ending in February 2026, when the inflationary effect peaked. Nearly 90% of Trump’s 2025 tariffs passed through to U.S. import prices almost immediately. Roughly a third of the increase in consumer goods prices came from American-made goods as manufacturers paid more for imported materials and raised their own prices. (Axios / Liberty Street Economics / Washington Post)
5/ Companies that Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have invested in have won more than $6 billion in federal contracts. Since then, Trump Jr.’s firm, 1789 Capital, took a stake in Anduril last year, the AI defense company has won 135 government contracts and received about $1.8 billion under those agreements. Yesterday, Trump announced another $2.9 billion in Navy support for an Anduril submarine-parts facility in Maryland. Other Trump Jr.-backed companies secured military contracts for rocket engines and automated submarine factories. Meanwhile, Foundation Future Industries won a $24 million contract for robotics startup, where Eric Trump is the chief strategy adviser. The brothers also hold indirect investments in drone maker Powerus, which also won an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million. (ABC News)
6/ Kimberly Guilfoyle reportedly urged a Trump donor to pay her $100,000 American Express bill. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” Trump Jr.’s former fiancée texted Eric Deters days before her Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she added. The messages also show Guilfoyle forwarding Deters’ tax dispute to the IRS commissioner and updating him on her efforts to lobby the Justice Department on his behalf. Deters never made the payment. (Wall Street Journal)
7/ ICE has investigated more than 150 voter-registration groups ahead of the midterm elections. It’s also considered deploying undercover agents to investigate groups suspected of helping noncitizens register to vote. Meanwhile, internal Department of Homeland Security documents show that ICE has collected nearly 100 million records as part of its effort to identify noncitizens illegally registering or voting. The records included 48.4 million supplied by Heather Honey, a senior DHS adviser who promoted false claims about the 2020 election, from unidentified “independent sources of information,” and another 50.6 million obtained from the Justice Department. Noncitizen voting is rare, and there is no credible evidence that it has changed the outcome of an election. (New York Times / CNN / Democracy Docket)
8/ The World Health Organization couldn’t assess the risk of a possible plague outbreak after a Russian anti-plague institute researcher died of pneumonia of unknown origin. WHO officials don’t know what caused her illness, but Russia denied any accident at the lab and maintained that “there are no epidemic risks,” despite quarantining or monitoring about 200 of her contacts. The WHO is also seeking clarification about unconfirmed reports that a second lab employee developing pneumonia of unknown cause. The U.S., meanwhile, sent Moscow a formal diplomatic warning over its failure to disclose details about the death. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the information Russia had shared as “still quite limited,” adding: “Maybe there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know.” Trump, however, maintained that the U.S. didn’t believe the incident involved a bioweapon: “We’re going to find out soon enough, but we don’t think so.” He acknowledged that “Russia is not saying much,” but repeated Moscow’s assurances that the situation was under control. Trump also claimed he had a call scheduled with Putin to discuss the incident. Kremlin, however, denied that a call had been arranged. (New York Times / CNN / Politico / Associated Press / Wall Street Journal / ABC News / Washington Post / CNBC / Bloomberg)
9/ Trump proposed turning his West Palm Beach golf club into a Camp David-type presidential retreat for future presidents and visiting foreign leaders. His attorney asked Palm Beach County, which owns the land, to provide a parcel to the federal government for a presidential residence. Trump would pay for construction, and his company would continue operating the private club and paying its lease. (Washington Post / The Hill / Mediaite)

sources.news_title: Ken Paxton Calls Trump's War in Iran His Campaign's 'Biggest Problem' in Latest Leaked-Audio Jab
sources.text:
Ken Paxton Calls Trump's War in Iran His Campaign's 'Biggest Problem' in Latest Leaked-Audio Jab
Oct. 7 2026, Published 3:46 p.m. ET
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton told donors last month that President Donald Trump's war in Iran, and the fuel prices that followed it, are "by far" the "biggest problem" in his Senate race.
The recording is the third leak from a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, RadarOnline.com can reveal.
Paxton Blames Trump's Iran War
Paxton, the Republican nominee against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, was asked what was dragging the campaign.
"It's not tariffs," he said in the audio clip obtained by a publication. "It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel."
He said those costs had pushed up food prices, and that affordability was why the campaign was "having a hard time with numbers."
Trump is scheduled to rally with him in San Antonio on Wednesday.
Paxton Claimed He Has 'No Control'
"We can't stop the war," Paxton continued. "I have no control over gas prices. So many of the factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions and I don't know what's behind some of the decisions."
He told the donors and lobbyists that the only lever he has is legislation, and he pointed to a tax-cut package with housing and health care deductions and an expanded child tax credit.
Other Paxton Campaign Leaks
The latest leak follows two other recordings from the same event in September.
As Radar previously reported, one clip included Paxton suggesting that Trump's midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9 and 10 hurt his standing.
"So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers," Paxton said. "Everybody's numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good."
In another clip, he said he'd never been in a race where he felt less control over the campaign or over which issues would matter, "because it's all coming, you know, from D.C."
He added, "I have to live with whatever I've got. So, it is a challenge."
Paxton's Corruption Precedes His Reputation
The Texas House impeached Paxton in 2023 on charges that included bribery and abuse of office, but the Senate acquitted him that September.
A separate securities fraud case filed in 2015 accused him of misleading investors in a Dallas-area tech company before he became attorney general. However, it ended without a trial.
In March 2024, he agreed to pay about $300,000 in restitution, perform 100 hours of community service, and complete 15 hours of legal ethics training. Prosecutors dropped three felony counts.

sources.news_title: New Audio Features Ken Paxton Saying Trump’s Policies Are “Dragging” Down His Campaign
sources.text:
Newly unearthed audio of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) reveals his frustration with President Donald Trump and his policies, which he views as dragging down his own campaign for U.S. senator.
The leaked audio, obtained by Axios, was recorded at a closed-door fundraising event in Washington, D.C.
In the recording, Paxton complained that he doesn’t “make the decisions” that impact his campaign, citing Trump policies that have been detrimental to the economy and likely resulted in voters shifting toward Democrats — including his opponent, state Rep. James Talarico (D).
When asked what’s “dragging” his campaign, Paxton responded, “It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel.”
The Republican Senate nominee also recognized that “people are feeling the pinch,” with rising fuel prices “driv[ing] up food prices and everything else.” Affordability is “by far our biggest problem,” Paxton added, and “why we’re having a hard time with [polling] numbers.”
Paxton then expressed doubts over Trump’s actions.
“So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said.
The revelation of this recording comes a week after other leaked audio from Paxton also made headlines. In that conversation, Paxton expressed similar misgivings over Trump, specifically faulting the president’s decision to have a “midterm convention.”
“To be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said in that conversation. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”
The reporting on these conversations comes as the president is scheduled to speak at a rally for Paxton in the Lone Star State on Wednesday evening.
Multiple polls show that Talarico is ahead of Paxton in the Texas race. In a recent YouGov poll of likely voters, Paxton garnered only 44 percent support, whereas Talarico secured 50 percent. The Democrat is also ahead of the Republican candidate in a New York Times/Siena poll, which shows a 51-45 margin favoring Talarico.
Trump is unlikely to see it Paxton’s way if he and other Republicans lose their midterm races. In an interview in August, Trump claimed that voters are “angry at Republicans,” but “not angry at me.”
Despite Trump’s claims, a recent NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist poll showed that 45 percent of voters said their preferences in the midterms should be viewed as a “vote against President Trump,” versus just 24 percent who said their preferences should be viewed as a vote for him.
The president currently has a net -27 point approval rating, according to an aggregate of polls compiled by FiftyPlusOne. Voters also prefer Democrats over Republicans in the midterm congressional races by eight points.

sources.news_title: Leaked audio: Frustrated Ken Paxton blames Trump for his campaign troubles
sources.text:
Ken Paxton is once again blaming Donald Trump for his campaign troubles. And once again, it was caught on tape.
In the latest recording, Paxton points directly to Trump’s war with Iran, high gas prices and rising diesel costs as major problems for his Senate campaign.
In the earlier recording, he blamed Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas for hurting his numbers.
And, apparently, there’s another thing coming from Washington that Paxton says he can’t control.
The latest audio was obtained by Axios, which reported that Paxton privately acknowledged that affordability is “by far our biggest problem” and that his campaign is “having a hard time with numbers.”
When asked what was hurting the campaign, Paxton dismissed tariffs.
“It’s not tariffs,” he said. “It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel.”
Paxton is running for Senate as a Republican and has been one of Trump’s political allies.
But behind closed doors, he’s now complaining that the president’s war with Iran and the resulting pressure on fuel prices are creating problems for his campaign.
And then he made another point that sounds increasingly familiar.
He doesn’t control it.
“So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable,” Paxton said. “I don’t make the decisions.”
That line takes on a little more weight when you remember what he said in the other leaked recording.
Just days earlier, audio from the same fundraiser revealed Paxton complaining that Trump’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas had hurt his campaign.
“When we did that convention, it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said, according to audio obtained by The New York Times.
He also complained that campaign decisions were coming from Washington and that he didn’t control many of them. Axios separately reported that Paxton said he didn’t control messaging and that decisions were coming from Washington.
Gas prices have been a political headache for Republicans as the Iran conflict has pushed fuel costs higher. Axios reported in July that the renewed fighting and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz had pushed the national average above $4 a gallon, while Republicans were increasingly worried about the political consequences.
Now Paxton is saying essentially the same thing behind closed doors.
The economy is hurting. Fuel prices are hurting. And his campaign is feeling it.
But there’s a particularly awkward wrinkle here.
Paxton has spent his political career aligning himself with Trump.
Trump endorsed him in the Republican primary, and Trump’s political operation has since poured substantial resources into helping his Senate campaign. Axios reported that a pro-Trump PAC spent $131 million in just 17 days supporting Paxton and attacking his Democratic opponent, James Talarico.
So Paxton is hardly operating independently of Trump.
Yet the leaked recordings show him privately identifying Trump’s political event and Trump’s Iran war as factors hurting his campaign.
And that’s what makes the pattern so striking.
Twice now, Paxton has been caught on tape describing problems for his Senate campaign — and twice, he has pointed fingers at Trump.

sources.news_title: Trump-backed Ken Paxton admits Iran war, fuel prices are hurting his Texas Senate bid
sources.text:
Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately acknowledged that the Iran war and rising fuel prices are creating difficulties for his campaign, telling donors and lobbyists that several factors affecting the race were beyond his control, according to Axios.
Paxton, Texas attorney general and a close ally of President Donald Trump, as per the report, made the remarks during a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, DC, last month.
Axios said it has obtained an audio recording of the meeting from an attendee who opposed Paxton and was granted anonymity because the event was private.
Asked what issues were weighing on his campaign, Paxton said the problem was not tariffs but the war and rising gasoline and diesel prices, according to the recording obtained by the news outlet.
He specifically pointed to diesel prices of more than $6 a gallon, saying higher fuel costs were being felt by consumers and were contributing to increased food prices and other expenses.
Paxton described affordability as the biggest problem facing his campaign and linked it to difficulties with his polling numbers.
When an attendee noted that Paxton could not stop the war, the Republican candidate agreed and said he had no control over gas prices.
He also acknowledged that several factors affecting a federal Senate race were outside his control.
“I don’t make the decisions,” Paxton said, according to the media outlet, adding that he did not know what was behind some of the decisions.
Paxton pointed to his proposed tax-cut plan as a way to address affordability concerns.
The plan includes new deductions related to housing and healthcare, as well as an expansion of the child tax credit, according to Axios.
“I’m just trying to figure out ways I can help people,” Paxton said, adding that his role would be to propose legislation.
The Paxton campaign rejected the significance of the comments, telling Axios that the attorney general was simply acknowledging the high cost of gasoline and diesel and the pressure those prices were putting on Texans.
The campaign said Trump was working to bring prices down and argued that Paxton would go to Washington to support those efforts while seeking to put more money into families’ pockets.
Trump is scheduled to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday.
Paxton is running against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after defeating Republican Senator John Cornyn in the May primary runoff.
A Talarico victory would mark the first time a Democrat has been elected to the US Senate from Texas since the 1980s.
Paxton has been among Trump's most loyal political allies. Trump backed Paxton during the Republican primary despite appeals from Senate Republicans to support Cornyn.

sources.news_title: Paxton blames poor performance on Iran war, gas prices
sources.text:
Paxton blames poor performance on Iran war, gas prices
HUNT VALLEY, Md. (TNND) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the reeling Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, is blaming his so-far poor performance on factors beyond his control.
Paxton has trailed his Democratic opponent in most polls over the past few months as he struggles to attract donors wary of his legal baggage and attachment to the GOP's unpopular governance. He was charged with fraud in a since-dropped case and impeached by state Republicans, all the while defending the Trump administration's legally dubious dealings.
He told a group of donors and lobbyists at a recent closed-door event that the Iran war, and its subsequent effect on fuel prices, is more to blame for his campaign issues.
"It's the war, it's the gas prices, it's diesel," he said in an audio clip published by Axios Wednesday. "When it's over $6 a gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch. So I'd say that's probably the biggest problem."
The average price for a gallon of diesel in Texas is $5.72, according to AAA data, but rates in many other states are well above $6. Many Texans are upset over fuel costs, but Paxton's legal problems also present a challenging obstacle on his road to the Senate.
Eighty-five percent of voters told The New York Times and Siena University last month they have heard of the attorney general's controversies, and 45 percent of that group said they'll consider those issues at the polls.
Paxton's spent valuable time defending himself against attacks by state Representative James Talarico, who's leaned heavily on an anti-corruption platform.
"You shouldn't believe anything a politician says, whether it's me or Ken Paxton. You should look at what we've done," Talarico said in a Fox News interview last month. "And if you look at Ken Paxton's history, he has spent his entire career enriching himself on the public's dime. I'll put my record up against Ken Paxton's every day of the week."
The National News Desk requested comment from the attorney general but hasn't received a response.
He's focused on Talarico's positions on cultural issues, which helped Republicans in 2024, when they took control of the Senate and White House and kept their House majority. The Democrat, Paxton says, is too far left for Texas's reliably red electorate.
"Texas is NOT California. James Talarico is the most radical Senate candidate our state has ever seen," Paxton said in a September call for donations. "Help us stop him before National Democrats turn Texas blue."

sources.text:
Ken Paxton Blames Iran War and High Fuel Prices for Voter Frustration in Leaked Audio
Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately pointed to the Iran war and rising fuel prices as major problems affecting voters and his campaign, according to newly leaked audio from a private fundraiser.
The recording was reportedly made during a September gathering with donors and lobbyists in Washington, D.C. Paxton was asked what issues were weighing most heavily on his campaign as he prepares to face Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in November.
Paxton rejected the idea that tariffs were primarily responsible for his difficulties. Instead, he pointed directly to the war, gasoline prices and the cost of diesel, arguing that higher transportation expenses are spreading throughout the economy.
“When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel,” Paxton said, “people are feeling the pinch.” He added that expensive fuel contributes to higher food prices and other household costs.
Paxton described affordability as the biggest challenge facing his campaign. He acknowledged that many of the factors influencing a federal race are outside the control of an individual Senate candidate, including energy prices and decisions involving the war.
“I don’t make the decisions,” Paxton said during the private discussion, adding that he did not know what was behind some of the decisions being made at the federal level.
The Paxton campaign downplayed the recording after it became public. A campaign representative said the attorney general was simply acknowledging what Texans already know about elevated gasoline, diesel and grocery prices while arguing that President Trump is working to reduce those costs.
Paxton also discussed his own economic proposals during the meeting. His agenda includes additional tax deductions involving housing and health care expenses as well as an expansion of the child tax credit, measures he says would leave families with more money.
The recording is the latest in a series of leaked private comments involving Paxton. Earlier audio captured him expressing frustration about the influence of Washington Republicans over his campaign and saying the Republican midterm convention in Dallas had negatively affected his numbers.
Trump has continued backing Paxton despite the leaked recordings. The president endorsed him over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn during the Republican primary and is scheduled to campaign alongside Paxton in San Antonio as Republicans work to hold the Texas Senate seat.
The Texas race has attracted significant national attention and spending as Paxton faces Talarico in the November election. Republicans have held both of the state’s U.S. Senate seats for decades, but both parties are pouring substantial resources into the contest.
Paxton’s latest comments highlight how energy prices and the economic effects of the Iran conflict have become prominent issues in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign. His campaign maintains that his focus remains on reducing costs and pursuing tax relief for Texas families.

sources.news_title: Ken Paxton 'said the quiet part out loud' in leaks. Will voters listen?
sources.text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s private remarks are becoming a storyline with less than a month to Election Day.
Paxton is coming off a dogfight of a primary race against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, a race which saw the three-term Texas Attorney General overcome previous scandals as he positioned himself as the ultimate MAGA Republican. Now pitted against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, the Republican machine has made a concerted effort to keep focus away from Paxton and instead lambast “Talafreako,” as he’s commonly called on airwaves.
But recent audio recordings have drawn Paxton back into the spotlight. One, a recording of a D.C. fundraiser verified by The New York Times, has Paxton saying Trump’s Dallas recent midterm convention “hurt his campaign,” an unfortunate misstep by a man once hailed as a “true MAGA warrior” by the president. Another, which leaked over the weekend and Politico published Monday morning, featured an even longer admission in another conversation with donors.
“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.,” Paxton said in the recording.
One attendee also told Politico that while Trump wasn’t named directly, “everyone in the room knew what he was talking about.”
‘What we all know’
Texas Democrats have pounced on the opportunity to slam Paxton. In a statement, Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Ryan Martin said Paxton’s latest remarks covered “what we all know.”
“Corrupt Ken Paxton admits behind closed doors what we all know: that he is a puppet being controlled by his billionaire megadonors and D.C. insiders,” Martin wrote. “Paxton’s entire disastrous campaign is run by D.C., not Texas, and now Paxton’s own words confirm it. Paxton is a fraud who only serves himself and the corrupt interests that back him, and it is exactly why Texans will be kicking him to the curb in November. Don’t D.C. our Texas, Ken.”
Paxton’s campaign has pushed back on the latest leak, with campaign spokesperson Nick Maddux telling the Observer in a statement that Paxton’s words were misinterpreted.
“Campaigns don’t coordinate with super PACs and that’s obviously what AG Paxton was referring to. AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority which is why he’s on the ground every day talking to Texans, raising money, and taking his message directly to the people including with his statewide television buy that started over this past weekend,” Maddux wrote.
Paxton’s campaign also accused the Times of releasing “manipulated nonsense” and told Fox 4 that he leads Talarico by three points in internal polls.
Paxton trails his opponent by six points in a recent New York Times/Sienna poll. Other polls have shown a swing toward Talarico in recent weeks, with analysts such as VoteHub now placing the Texas Senate race in the ‘lean Dem’ column.
Turnout and messaging
Parker Hevron, a political science professor at Texas Woman’s University, said he “doesn’t know how much more damage” can be done to Paxton’s image amid highly publicized scandals. The Republican nominee was impeached by a GOP-majority Texas House in 2023 and is currently in the middle of a divorce with Texas Sen. Angela Paxton, who accused her husband of 38 years of adultery in the divorce filings.
But even as Paxton’s “skeletons in the closet,” as Hevron described them, have become well known, he said the second leak could still be potentially more damaging for his campaign.
“That’s really different than not only telling Texans that somebody else is making his campaign decisions, which I think in a state that values its sense of independence and kind of iconoclasm, that’s not going to go over well. But then, you know, leveraging that with the fact that the president and, particularly, the Republican Party right now is pretty unpopular, I think that’s kind of a double whammy.”
Trump’s approval ratings sit near record lows amid an unpopular war in Iran and lingering economic issues that he had pledged to address while running for a non-consecutive second term in 2024. Some Republicans have expressed concern about placing such an unpopular incumbent at the center of the GOP’s messaging, while candidates in some states have also backed off. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott recently announced he would not attend a San Antonio rally with Trump due to scheduling conflicts. Hevron said Abbott “is not safe” in his race against Gina Hinojosa and added that his cancellation could stem from concerns about Trump’s influence.
Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said Paxton’s first leak all but confirmed those sentiments about Trump’s involvement. Before deriding the convention, Paxton was asked, “Do you think he is a drag?” although it is unclear who the speaker meant.
“Paxton has said the quiet part out loud that there are worries that Donald Trump is not as big a draw as expected, and that it is a liability for Republicans to have him fronting the ticket even rhetorically, so I think that’s the biggest kind of thing that this lets us know,” Rottinghaus said.
With the Republican primary still lingering in some voters’ minds, Rottinghaus said turnout will be a major deciding factor in the election and that Paxton’s leaks could hurt his standing outside of the core MAGA base, although they have come early enough in the cycle for Paxton to recover. He added that the Republican base can be expected to show up in solid numbers, but some moderates who may have voted for Cornyn and independent voters could split their ticket or stay home entirely, creating a path to victory for Talarico.
The Latino vote, which swung to the right in 2022 and 2024, is also expected to play a pivotal role in the race. An early September poll by the Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision found that Talarico leads Paxton 63% to 30% among the key demographic, which represents a third of the Texas electorate.
Rottinghaus said Republican messaging has been “fractured” throughout the campaign and has now been blown off course by Paxton’s leaks, which puts even more pressure on his camp to take control of the narrative, although he is unsure which approach could work given the apparent ineffectiveness of negative ads against Talarico.
“So for Paxton, the question is not just how do we respond to these leaks, but what do we want to talk about that’s not these leaks? And I’m not sure they know what that is right now,” he said. “And as Paxton said, it’s really kind of dictated by what’s going on in D.C. So who knows what kind of politics they want to churn up?”
Early Wednesday morning, Axios released a third leaked recording in which Paxton said gas prices have been “by far” the biggest obstacle to his campaign. He also named the Iran War as another leading issue “dragging” his messaging, even though Trump has been insistent in defending the conflict. Polling by the Texas Politics Project has found that 36% of Texans strongly oppose the war, with a majority concerned about rising gas prices and cost of living issues tied to Trump’s escalation.
Paxton is set to appear with the president at the San Antonio rally later tonight.

Texas Attorney General and Senate candidate Ken Paxton

Yet another leaked recording of Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton has landed.
“It’s the war, it’s gas prices.... It’s over $6 a gallon for diesel,” Paxton said at a donor meeting when asked what issues were “dragging” on him and his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios. “People are feeling that pinch. This is at least the third time Paxton has unknowingly been recorded sending either subliminal or direct messages to Trump in recent days. This amount of leaks from one of the GOP’s most important Senate campaigns this cycle feels shocking, especially when each leak is Paxton indirectly blaming Trump for low poll numbers and affordability issues that he has to cover for. It seems obvious that he’s upset with the Trump administration—as he keeps confirming to donors over and over again.
Trump, 80, Claims Iran War Ended Eight Months Before He Started It
Donald Trump made the bonkers claim in front of a dead silent crowd.
Win McNamee/Getty Images
President Donald Trump falsely claimed Tuesday that his military campaign against Iran ended eight months before he started it.
In the latest installment of Senior Moment or Shocking Admission?, the president offered an outrageous defense against anyone complaining that his so-called “six-week war” had stretched on for more than seven months.
“We really ended it as soon as the B2 bombers hit, because that was the end of their nuclear [program], that was 95 percent of the reason we did it. Maybe 100 percent,” he said.
Trump was referring to a series of strikes using “bunker buster” bombs on three of Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. That was a full eight months before he ordered attacks in March 2026.
Clearly, those strikes didn’t actually end the war in the Middle East.
This particular comment is concerning in light of the Trump administration officials who have previouslycontradicted Trump’s claims that Iran’s nuclear program presented any imminent threat to national security.
Why the Hell Is Kash Patel’s FBI Making Campaign Ads?
Patel has turned the bureau into a P.R. agency for Donald Trump.
Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images
Kash Patel’s FBI slammed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a wildly partisan, and likely illegal, propaganda video Tuesday.
In a two-minute video posted on social media, the supposedly nonpartisan agency decried “democratic socialist leaders” for calling to defund the police. The video included footage of multiple Democrats calling to defund the police, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, current and former Representatives Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez, Cori Bush, and Ilhan Omar, and, of course, El-Sayed, who is running for office in November’s midterm elections.
“Not reform. Defund the police as policy,” the video’s narration stated. “As the path they said would keep you safer. In the cities that led the charge, the street told a different story. What followed was a complete failure.” There is little data that supports this, and crime rates have been in decline for years.
The video praised Patel’s leadership, and touted a major increase in the arrest of violent criminals. It’s worth noting that Patel has reportedly instituted a policy of double-counting these arrests with those made by other law enforcement agencies, and has faced criticism for his disastrous leadership.
Federal law clearly prohibits the use of government funds for campaign purposes, partisan political messaging, and propaganda. A wildly inaccurate attack ad against a Democratic candidate would more than count under all three of these categories—and it’s more than a little ironic that the FBI’s latest video preaching law and order likely violated federal law. But under the Trump administration, it’s clear that nothing will be done.
Recently, the Trump administration has used at least 5.6 million taxpayer dollars to buy a series of at least 15 campaign-style advertisements touting the president’s agenda ahead of November’s midterm elections. In order to make and air those videos, the Trump administration stole the money from the Department of Homeland Security, specifically from U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Trump is visiting the site and speaking about the investment on Tuesday and is barring Moore from speaking, the governor told The Baltimore Banner.
“That’s correct,” Moore said to reporters following a debate with his Republican gubernatorial opponent, Dan Cox. “I will not be there later on today. This was going to be a deal that we helped break. This is going to be the largest private investment that we have seen in over a decade inside the state of Maryland.”
“If the president of the United States wants to bring the circus in town and tell me that I’m not allowed to speak, despite the fact we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to the work of the people of Maryland,” Moore added.
An unnamed White House official told CNN that Moore was “graciously” invited as a guest but didn’t deny that Trump was blocking the governor from speaking.
“It’s unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multibillion-dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump,” the official said.
Other Maryland Democrats, such as Representative Johnny Olszewski Jr., whose district encompasses the new facility, were scheduled to speak but pulled out after news that Moore wouldn’t be allowed to make remarks.
Trump has never been a fan of Moore, uninviting him from a bipartisan dinner that included nearly every other state governor, accusing him of committing electoral fraud, and blaming him for a sewage spill in the Potomac River. Meanwhile, Moore is leading his Trump-supporting Republican opponent, Dan Cox, in polls for November’s election.
Man Arrested After Impersonating ICE Agent at Polling Site
The man said he wanted to “see people’s reactions.”
Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe/Getty Images
A man was arrested Sunday for allegedly impersonating an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer and intimidating voters at a Miami polling site for Brazil’s presidential elections.
According to his arrest report, 46-year-old Danilo Alves Silva was aggressively pacing between polling locations and interacting with people who seemed to be “in fear” of him at Miami-Dade College’s Kendall Campus. He was wearing an ICE costume that he allegedly purchased on Amazon, complete with a blue “ICE raid jacket,” an ICE hat, sunglasses, jeans, and tactical boots, according to the arrest report. His face was covered with a camouflage mask and he was speaking into a handheld radio.
When confronted by detectives and sheriff’s deputies from the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office, Silva said that he was wearing the costume “so that I can come here to see people’s reactions.”
“The people were gathered and were clearly in fear that, as they portrayed it, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement ICE agent was interfering with their election, possibly deporting individuals,” the arrest report reads.
Silva claimed that he himself was a Brazilian voter and he changed into the ICE costume after casting his ballot, apparently just to see what would happen. To make matters worse, he attempted to bribe law enforcement officers after his arrest, telling them, “I will get you paid if you let me go.”
Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is seen by many as a referendum on President Trump’s influence in South America, pitting right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of disgraced Trump ally Jair Bolsonaro, against leftist incumbent Lula da Silva. The election will move to a runoff in October.
This arrest comes amid widespread anxiety that ICE or other federal law enforcement officials at the polls may interfere in voters’ ability to cast their ballots on America’s Election Day, less than a month away. FBI Director Kash Patel himself hasn’t ruled out sending the bureau’s agents to voting locations in November, ostensibly to prevent “violations of the law,” though their presence would more likely frighten and intimidate voters. Impersonators like Silva could have the same effect.

sources.news_title: GOP 'laying groundwork' to abandon Paxton after 3rd incendiary audio leak
sources.text:
The Republicans could be privately considering how much longer they should continue to spend money on Ken Paxton's Senate campaign, as a third leak of an incendiary audio recording threatens to make the MAGA candidate an even greater expense for the party.
The most recent recording, which Axios released on Wednesday, shows Paxton blaming his difficulties in the race against Democrat James Talarico on President Donald Trump's policy towards Iran, high fuel prices and decisions beyond his control.
“Republican Senate campaign committee is def laying the groundwork to abandon him,” X user David Leake wrote in response.
The response comes at a time when Republicans are already having private discussions about what will happen when the large amount of spending for Paxton that is aligned with Trump runs out.
Politico previously reported that senior Republican members of Congress and other GOP officials have been asking Trump's team for more money for Texas. However, following the release of Paxton's first recorded message, some people started to worry that MAGA Inc. might cease its spending when its current advertising reservations expire on October 12.
A Trump associate stated that MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups intended to spend around $45 million by that date, although they were still deciding how much additional money to commit afterward.
Irritation towards Paxton has led some Republicans to make exceptionally direct evaluations.
“There seems to be very little strategy there,” one Republican senator told Politico. “Sometimes, I think [Paxton] wants to lose.”
One Republican senator compared the race to a “five-alarm fire,” and a Republican campaign strategist called Paxton’s campaign a “slow-moving car crash." Outside spending by Republicans in the race is expected to surpass $200 million.
This latest leak is unlikely to make the decision any easier.
When asked what was bothering him politically, Paxton told his donors, “It’s not tariffs. ... It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel.”
Paxton described affordability as "by far our biggest problem" and complained that the factors influencing the race were outside his control.
“I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t ... know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said.
This is the third recording to have come out of the September fundraiser.
One captured Paxton saying that Trump's Dallas midterm convention "dropped our numbers," and another stated that he had “never been in a race where I felt less control” since the campaign decisions were coming from Washington.
Trump subsequently called Paxton a “pain in the ass” while campaigning for him, though he continued urging Republicans to elect him.
Paxton's campaign rejected the latest recording, stating that Texans are already aware that fuel prices are high.
Since Republican operatives were already discussing how much additional money to send after October 12, a third leak has given those who were thinking about when to stop the rescue operation yet another reason to change their minds.

sources.news_title: LEAKED AUDIO: Ken Paxton Privately Points to Trump’s Iran War as ‘By Far Our Biggest Problem’
CNN data analyst Harry Enten warns President Donald Trump and Ken Paxton ‘both stink,’ says the Republican Texas Senate candidate is ‘the worst of the worst’
sources.text:
Ken Paxton has a problem heading into the Texas Senate race, according to Harry Enten.
The CNN data analyst said voters have a negative view of the Republican and that Paxton is “the worst of the worst.”
Donald Trump is traveling this week to Texas to campaign for the Senate nominee, but Enten questioned whether his support would actually help Paxton with voters.
‘Bit of a drag’
While Trump is trying to help the party amid low polling, leaked audio showed Paxton criticizing the president’s appearance at the midterm convention last week.
During a private fundraiser, Paxton was asked whether he thought Trump had become “a little bit of a drag.”
“So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”
Legal trouble
Despite their differences, Enten said Trump and Paxton have one thing in common.
“The Texans, you know what they say?” he asked. “They both stink! They both stink!” the analyst said of Paxton and Trump. “And Ken Paxton especially stinks. He’s the worst of the worst.”
Paxton was impeached by the Texas House over corruption allegations, but was later acquitted by the Senate.
His wife, Angela, also filed for divorce on “biblical grounds” of adultery.
Although the two are no longer together, she has urged voters to keep the seat in Republican hands.
Bad polling
Enten then brought up the numbers to show how voters view Paxton.
“I mean, just look at this key GOP Senate nominee’s popularity. Look who’s at the bottom of this list. It’s Ken Paxton! He’s at minus-16 points. The worst of the worst,” he said.
The analyst continued, “None of these other key Republican Senate nominees are positive. But yet Ken Paxton beats them all in the negative direction. Minus-16 points, worse than in Ohio, minus-11. Minus eight in Michigan, minus-seven in Maine, minus-two in Iowa.”
“Ken Paxton is by far the least popular Republican Senate nominee in a key state. When you look at all the polling, Texans simply put — they hate him!”
More unpopular
“Congratulations to Ken Paxton! You have done it. You are the least popular Texas GOP Senate nominee this century,” Enten quipped.
“You’ve managed to do it. And when I was looking at the data, no one else was even in the negative. And you’re at minus-16 points at this point,” he added.
“This is record-breaking for Texas. Texas is normally a Republican state, almost always the Republican Senate nominee is in positive territory. But Ken Paxton just isn’t in negative territory. He is deep in negative territory, deep under the Gulf of Mexico, or again, in Trump’s language, the Gulf of America.”
